chunks: Specifying a BLDC motor. The question: How do you spec a BLDC motor?
Specifying a BLDC motor means working backward from the load. Work out the torque and speed you need, and the supply you have.
Then choose a motor whose constants fit, check it does not overheat, and add the practical details such as sensors, size and mounting.
Think of choosing a car engine for a trailer. You first decide how heavy the load is and how fast you must tow it.
Then you check the engine can deliver that power without overheating, and the fuel tank (here, the battery) can keep up.
The analogy has one gap: with a motor, the battery voltage also limits top speed, because the back-EMF must stay below it.
The spec flows from the application to the motor, and loops back if any check fails. The voltage check and thermal check are the two that most often change the choice.
Mechanical power: torque times angular speed, P equals T omega . Torque constant ( K t ): newton-meters (N·m) of torque per amp of current.
Back-EMF: the voltage the spinning motor makes. Duty: the fraction of time the controller's switches are on. It sets the average voltage the motor sees.
Headroom: spare supply voltage left over for acceleration and disturbances. Continuous rating: the torque the motor can hold without overheating.

That is the whole idea: torque sets current, speed sets voltage.
"I work backwards from the load: continuous and peak torque, speed, duty and supply voltage. Power is T omega .
I choose K t so that the current at continuous torque is within the continuous rating and the back-EMF plus IR at top speed is under about 85% of the supply.
Then I check heating, I to the 2R times thermal resistance, and peak torque against the current limit.
Finally I check sensors, pole count and frequency, size, bearings, environment and the controller."
